summary: The European Commission confirmed that the political deal on the EU AI Act lets it adapt the rules for "general purpose" AI (GPAI) over time, including updating the initial 10^25 FLOPs threshold for high-impact models. The generic term was chosen to futureproof the law, and an AI Office plus a scientific panel will help set thresholds and spot new risks. High risk GPAIs face systemic-risk obligations, others face transparency and watermarking duties, and the full law likely won't apply until 2026.
one_line: The Commission says the EU AI Act's general purpose AI rules, including the 10^25 FLOPs threshold, can be updated over time via an AI Office and delegated acts.
key_facts: The EU Act uses the term "general purpose" AI models and systems rather than "foundational" or "frontier" to avoid being tied to a specific technology such as transformer based machine learning.
A Commission official said the general purpose AI model would be GPT-4 and the general purpose AI system would be ChatGPT, in which GPT-4 is integrated.
The agreed draft sets the bar for a GPAI to have "high impact capabilities" at 10^25 FLOPs of training compute.
The Commission said 10^25 FLOPs is only an "initial threshold" that it can update through implementing/delegating acts, and it could go up or down.
The FLOPs threshold is meant to be combined over time with "other benchmarks" developed by the AI Office, a new expert oversight body within the Commission.

Makers of GPAIs must self assess whether their models meet the FLOPs threshold and thus fall under rules for GPAIs "with systemic risk"; the Commission would not say whether GPT-4 or Gemini are captured.
High risk GPAIs must assess and mitigate systemic risks, proactively testing outputs for effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights or society.

Low tier GPAIs face lighter transparency requirements, including watermarking generative AI outputs using state of the art technology; the Commission noted watermarking works better for video and audio than text.

GPAI makers must respect EU copyright rules including the machine readable text and data mining opt-out in the EU Copyright Directive, and the open source carve-out does not exempt them from copyright obligations.
The AI Office has no budget or headcount defined yet, and will work with a new scientific advisory panel that can flag risks from models not captured by the FLOP threshold.
The final text is likely to emerge in January or February, and the AI Act likely won't be in full force until some time in 2026.

High risk rules for GPAIs apply 24 months after entry into force, while prohibited uses such as social scoring and Clearview AI-style selfie scraping apply six months after, potentially in the second half of 2024.
Talks to agree the deal lasted 38 hours and ended Friday night; the EU will push GPAIs to follow codes of practice via the AI Pact in the meantime.
